reviews.review:
Mahjong Pretty Girls Battle takes traditional Japanese riichi mahjong and packages it inside a colorful anime presentation built around a large cast of female characters. Developed and published by Zoo Corporation, it was released in 2015 and is fundamentally a legitimate mahjong game rather than a simple tile-matching puzzle. Its anime styling may be the first thing that catches the eye, but underneath that presentation is a fairly traditional interpretation of Japanese mahjong that expects players to understand its rules and strategic possibilities.

The game revolves around authentic riichi mahjong matches against computer-controlled opponents. Players draw and discard tiles while attempting to construct valid hands, balancing the pursuit of valuable combinations against the need to avoid dangerous discards. Concepts such as yaku, riichi declarations, open and closed hands, sequences, triplets, and defensive play are all relevant. There are also settings for certain rule variations, which gives experienced players some flexibility in configuring matches according to their preferences. This makes the game considerably more substantial than its playful presentation might initially suggest.

Where the experience struggles is accessibility. Japanese mahjong has a complicated collection of rules, scoring systems, and valid hand requirements, and the game is not particularly effective at teaching all of them to a complete beginner. Someone who already understands riichi mahjong can quickly appreciate what is being simulated, but newcomers may wonder why apparently complete hands cannot win or why particular decisions are strategically poor. It can still function as a place to practice, but learning the fundamentals through an outside tutorial before playing will make the experience considerably less frustrating.

The major personality comes from a roster of 23 characters. Instead of following a single theme, the cast includes high school students, idols, fantasy characters, a samurai-inspired fighter, a ninja, a nun, devils, goddesses, and even animal-inspired characters given human forms. The deliberately exaggerated selection keeps the visual presentation lively and provides an entertaining contrast to the methodical nature of mahjong. Each character is also voiced in Japanese, with vocal reactions accompanying victories, defeats, and important moments during matches.

Despite the suggestive character designs and mature presentation, players should not expect an elaborate adult game or an extensive visual novel. The character artwork primarily serves as decoration around the mahjong matches. There is no central undressing mechanic or nudity-based progression. The personalities, voices, and illustrations give the matches flavor, but the real attraction remains playing mahjong. Anyone buying it exclusively for its character artwork may therefore find the content relatively limited, while mahjong enthusiasts are more likely to appreciate the actual substance underneath it.

The single-player structure is both comfortable and restrictive. Playing against AI makes it easy to start a match without depending on other people, and different opponents can encourage slightly different approaches. It is suitable for practicing hands, experimenting with strategies, and becoming more familiar with riichi rules at your own pace. Character progression and statistical tracking provide additional reasons to continue playing. However, the lack of online multiplayer is a significant weakness because mahjong becomes especially interesting when human opponents introduce unpredictable strategies, bluffing, risk management, and changing patterns of behavior.

Visually, the game is functional but clearly reflects its age. The mahjong table communicates the essential information without unnecessary complexity, while character portraits provide most of the visual identity. The Japanese voice work gives the presentation considerably more energy than the graphics alone could provide. Some terminology and interface decisions can feel awkward, particularly for English-speaking players, and the overall presentation lacks the refinement expected from more modern digital mahjong titles. Fortunately, its modest technical requirements mean it is not demanding on conventional PC hardware.

Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Unsupported. SteamOS can run the game, but Valve's compatibility assessment indicates a problem involving graphics configuration that prevents the title from meeting Steam Deck requirements. This means it should not be purchased specifically for Deck use with the expectation of a smooth, officially supported experience. Players willing to experiment may have some success, but desktop Windows remains the safer environment for playing it.

As a complete package, this is a niche title that succeeds most when judged as an anime-themed riichi mahjong simulator. The authentic rules, configurable elements, sizable character roster, Japanese voices, and straightforward single-player matches provide enough substance for enthusiasts who enjoy practicing against AI. Its shortcomings are equally noticeable: limited instruction for newcomers, dated presentation, no human multiplayer, and officially Unsupported Steam Deck compatibility all restrict its broader appeal.

For players who already understand Japanese mahjong and enjoy anime aesthetics, there is a surprisingly competent game underneath the provocative marketing. Beginners can still enjoy it, but they should expect a considerable learning curve that the game itself does not fully address. The colorful cast makes repeated matches more entertaining, while the underlying rules preserve the strategic depth that makes riichi mahjong compelling. It is neither the most accessible introduction to mahjong nor the most feature-rich digital version available, but within its specific niche it offers an entertaining combination of serious tile strategy and deliberately playful presentation.

Rating: 7/10
